This is a great idea: the combination of a USB 3.0 hub and a gigabit adapter. It's a perfect space-saving option -- the overall size is just a bit larger than my gigabit adapter and I get 3 USB 3.0 ports as a bonus!

The build quality is very good. It seems odd to use the word "stylish" to describe such a device, but this is quite stylish -- the case is black with a steel gray brushed top (which looks like metal, but I believe it is plastic). The case is sturdy and has tight seams, and the USB and RJ45 ports are well-anchored. The connection cable is short (about one foot long) but very stout with an well-made USB connector on the PC end.

Setup is quick and easy. The hub portion is a straight plus-and-play install on Win 7 (and, I would imagine, other Windows versions as well). The Ethernet adapter requires drivers, which are supplied on an included CD-ROM (which I'm pleased to report is a full-size CD rather than those mini ones which are such a pain to use).

The hub is passive (no external power) so there are limitations as to what it can support. I didn't have any problems using it with low power draws, such as thumb drives.

It comes with a brief, but well-written user guide.

Well-made, works great, and a easy, compact way to add two different functions to a laptop (or any other PC). Highly recommend.

I really love the Moshi iVisor "black border" screen protectors. They go on quickly, and bubble-free, because the protector is made of stiff plastic (for easy handling), and has adhesive only under the black portions (to avoid trapping dust motes in the backlit part of the screen). Because the screen protector is stiff, you can pick it up easily for do-overs until you're completely satisfied with the positioning.

As other reviewers have noted, this crystal-clear MOSHI IVISOR SCREEN PROTECTOR FOR KINDLE VOYAGE is highly reflective. I don't like matte-finish screen protectors at all, so I don't mind this. When I'm reading under a lamp or light source that causes mirror-like reflections, I simply adjust the angle at which I'm holding the Voyage. (In truth, you don't really need a screen protector for a Kindle Voyage or Paperwhite, if you have a simple case that protects it from scratches, such as the [[ASIN:B00MVUR3DY OMOTON Kindle Voyage Smart Case Cover]], or the [[ASIN:B00IU7CLD4 Incipio Top Folio Cover for Kindle Voyage]]).

My biggest concern when I installed this screen protector, was whether the stiff plastic would interfere with the Voyage's haptic page-turn feature. (A feature that you don't know you need until you experience it.) Happily, it does NOT. The Voyage's haptic page-turn continues to work perfectly after the protector goes on.

This screen protector took me about 10 minutes to install, including several repositioning do-overs. If you want to remove the protector for any reason, it leaves no residue behind. A microfiber cloth for cleaning the screen prior to applying the screen protector is included in the package.

Perhaps if the sound was better, or if the price was lower, these would be great headphones. The design is slick, and actually comes fully black-gray brand new (I know they "customize" over the years, but the blue on the cans in the Amazon picture threw me off).
The stretchiness is great, and I don't fear that the headphones would break easily if, say, someone accidentally sat on them. Nonetheless, I do have some gripes.

First, the sound is absolutely awful for $100. There was some tinny noise, and because the headphones have a hard time adjusting to my skull, I couldn't get the right position for the full sound effect. It's a shame that headphones of this price can't even beat my $20 Sennheisers (which is no jab at my beloved Sennheisers). Another issue I had is with the cord. I understand that it's certainly non-tangable, but it comes with a longer cord that makes absolutely no sense. The longer cord isn't the major issue, though; it's the short cord that extends from the headphones: it's so short, it can't attach to *anything* without requiring the longer cord. Maybe if you were on your bed and the iPod/music device was on your chest it would work, but I imagine people aren't buying these cans for bed use. The longer cord is absolutely fundamental to using, so I don't know why they even bothered separating it from the cans themselves. They should've made the shorter cord longer and the longer cord slightly shorter.

While the design is superb, I'd look elsewhere if you want good sound quality.

Considering the price, I'm giving this little cam 4.5 stars. The half star off is for a user manual that is not as clear as it could be, and for the non-existent buttons mentioned therein.

As Sean Carter wrote elsewhere on this page,this cam is small, cheap, and "set-it-and-forget-it".

I opened the box (which contained everything in the parts listed in the product description), took the stuff out, inserted a 16GB San Disk class 10 microSD plugged the camera in, and had it working in no time. I set the resolution to 720, set the time and date, and left the other stuff pretty much at factory default.

The bracket is dead easy to mount (vac cup). I ran the power cord up into the roof liner, down the inner rubber gasket of the A-pillar, then used a couple of clips to hide it under the bottom of the instrument panel. It comes out on the driver's side center console and plugs into the power port. I used black duct tape to cover the massive, glowing red LED that is on the plug.

So, basically, once you set it up you just leave it plugged in. It comes on when the car is turned on (or the key is turned to Accsy). Note that the cam will stop recording after a few seconds of no motion - like at stop signs, traffic signals, etc. So you may want to set it so it runs all the time.

It comes off the bracket fairly easily, so you can take it indoors and connect it to a computer to view the video. I connected it to a WIndows 8 laptop and the camera came on and queried if I wanted to use it as storage or as a cam. Since I wanted to playback the video I had just shot, I selected storage.

WIndows recognized it as a removable drive. The video is AVI format, stored in DCIM sub-folders within dated folders.. I played the videos back on the PC. Didn't really look for details, so I'll have to check again for things like license plates, etc. The first couple of videos were very fuzzy. After I took the factory protective film off of the lens it shot very nice clips.

The sound is very soft.

Again, this is an inexpensive camera, but it does every thing it's supposed to do.

* * * * * tl:dr;

Pros: Cheap, Easy to install, set up, use;

Cons: Sound is very soft;

Idiot point: Don't forget to take the protective cellophane off of the lens.

I really like this TV. So why 4 stars instead of 5? Well let me start with what is great about this TV and then we will get into why I dropped it a star. The price is amazing of course. We have a 2012 59 inch top of the line Samsung Plasma and the picture on the Vizio is quite a bit sharper and brighter. It has replaced the Samsung as our go to Blue Ray movie night TV. So to this point we have a TV that is well priced and provides a great picture. So lets move on to the bad. Viewing angle. In our living room a couch sits directly in front of the Vizio. From the couch the picture is AMAZING. Off at about a 35 degree angle sits a recliner and the picture loses a lot of color, brightness and sharpness as viewed from the chair. It is not a horrible picture from the chair but it is quite a difference from straight on. The other is the somewhat slow response from the Vizio smart TV system. Compared to hooking up a Roku the initial start up and response is much slower. Of course if you are going to hook up a Roku then this is no big deal. If you do not have viewing angle concerns and are hooking up a Roku then I think you will absolutely love this amazing bargain.

I was trying to setup a studio for a multi-cam live Q&A web-broadcast, and this unit came highly recommended. Turns out this might not be the best choice, and the whole experience sort of leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
First the good:
The functionality of this device really impressed me! All I wanted was a live HDMI switch that would let me keep the audio separate (so it would be live regardless of camera active) and wouldn't blank the display when swapping inputs (which consumer hdmi switches do, as the connection re-negotiates). This unit goes far beyond that, using industry standard production controls for cuts and cross fades, title / graphic overlays, and even some basic Chroma Keying for doing live green screen (that was a surprise!). The little LCD is pretty neat too.
And now, THE BAD:
THERE IS NO HDMI OUTPUT. It only supports SDI, which no one mentioned to me when I said I wanted to toggle between HDMI sources. There is an HDMI preview which shows you multi-view (all the cameras in a grid), but no regular HDMI output. Only SDI, which is ridiculous to me. You have the HDMI port there, at least give us the option to choose whether it is multi-view or program out! Black Magic claims they didn't offer the HDMI out because the connection isn't reliable, so they want to push SDI as the output. But that isn't acceptable, the hardware is there, give us a choice! The result of this stream is going to an internet broadcaster which supports an HDMI input only! Now I'd need to purchase yet another accessory to convert the final product back into an HDMI signal so it can get where it needs to go.
Oh, and speaking of additional accessories that need to be purchased, THE BOX LACKS A POWER CORD. You have to source your own. That seems silly, its such an inexpensive thing that you expect to be there. Thankfully I have a cord from an old lighting accessory that I don't use anymore, but it seemed very odd that it was missing to me. Then, it did not come with a setup guide or instructions, only an SD card. That's fine, going green and all that, but I put it in my laptop and it came up blank. So now I have to find the software and manual myself. And at first, I found what I thought was the correct manual via Google only to realize it was for a different version of their ATEM products.
I know this is an inexpensive product for what it is, but let's be serious for a moment- it still costs nearly $1,000. For that amount of money, how much could it really cost to throw in a power cable and printed manual? $5? 10? Compared to the price of the unit, that's close to nothing. I also know that the buttons on front are because it is designed to be rack-mountable, but when you're setting this up on the fly and try to put on a tabletop, the controls are just awkward. It would have been a lot nicer ergonomically to have some controls on the top instead of the front side. But now that's just nitpicking. At the end of the day, I feel like this device is frustratingly close to what I was looking for, but the experience has been pretty crummy so far.

I've had these earbuds for a few months now and thought I'd revise my review.

My main gripe with these expensive but ultimately underwhelming earbuds is that they make a "thwomping" sound inside your ear drum whenever you jog or walk fast with them. I was at the gym recently and the sound of the earbuds jostling about in my ears was distracting. I don't recall ever having that problem with cheaper earbuds. This sound persisted even after I customized the buds to fit the shape of my ear.

On the positive side, the sound is decent though the bass and treble weren't that impressive. Its most effective feature was the noise-cancelling feature, which effectively blocked out any other noise. It worked so well that I would never use these buds while driving, crossing traffic or walking alone home late at night. With the spate of iPhone robberies, it's better to be able to hear a stranger's footsteps behind you. It's perfect, however, when you're on a subway or a bus and you want to block out that annoying person next to you who insists on complaining about her day.

The set includes a microphone for your iphone, which I don't use that much but works well enough - I heard my friend's voice on the other end of the line in very crisp, clear tones.

What's convenient is that the buds work with even the oldest ipods around. From the classic 2009 model to the most up to date Nano. Sony was smart to do this - that means a lot of people, not just techies with the most up-to-date devices, can use this. As an example, a friend of mine still has a working iPod mini (don't laugh, he's a Luddite!) and we tested the headset on that too. Surprisingly, it worked! - though the volume controls did not work with such an old, outdated model.

Another convenience is the location of the controls, which are located on a box located on the cord, which prevents you from having to reach all the way down to your iPod or iPhone to adjust the volume. My second favorite feature is the included clip, which allows me to wind up any slack on the cord and prevent it from getting tangled easily. In the past, I've killed so many earbuds because I pulled too hard on the cord by accident, so this is a welcome feature.

This deluxe model includes a pouch that offers an array of different sized earbuds - one set is noise-cancelling, while the other isn't. This is overkill, though. I tried out different sets of buds but none of them fit just right. And the "thwoping" sound I mentioned earlier still remained.

So I have mixed feelings about this product. The "thwomping" (sucking) sound is its biggest drawback for me, as the buds work best when you don't move around a lot.

IMPORTANT ADVICE... do not thread the mini ball head onto anything too tightly. This stand is actually fine, it's the cheap ball head that has given me headaches. The ball head has a... I'm not sure what the technical term is for this kind of bolt, but lets call it a "dual bolt." 1/4 bolt is threaded inside a bigger bolt, I presume 1/2. I threaded a mini projector onto this thing, I guess a little too tight. When I unthreaded the projector, the 1/4 bolt was stuck, meaning it was unthreading WITH the projector. So the 1/4 bolt came off the 1/2 bolt. You would think that all it takes are some pliers, but surprisingly, pliers even with teeth, have a hard time gripping this bolt. I had to use my drill press vise to get it off.

To properly use that ball head, you want to thread it onto whatever device you're using, but don't thread it on too tight like me. Then tighten with the lower knob. You might think, this reviewer isn't using common sense. I don't think so at all. Anybody would like his/her electronics threaded securely. The amount of strength I used was reasonable. The issue lies in that inner 1/4 bolt not being secured enough inside that bigger bolt. But I fixed that. Once I was able to unthread the projector from the vise... with the 1/4 bolt now free, but secured by the vise, I then took the ball head body to the vise and threaded the bigger bolt onto the 1/4 bolt a "wee bit" tighter than the manufacturer did.

If you don't have drill press vise like I do, then you better be extra careful using this. 3-Stars.

This weird little tripod is a useful addition to the gear of any amateur or hobby photographer with a DSLR and the inspiration to take breath-taking and/or unusual photographs. (I'm using it with a Nikon D7000)

Pros:

1. Light and portable. If you don't have a side pocket on your camera bag, just wrap it around a strap or loop.
2. Flexible. As advertised, the legs can be bent into loops and angles for getting shots from weird angles. It can also be wrapped around posts, tree branches, bench rails etc.
3. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring a stable camera almost level with ledges or sideways attached to a tree. However, you can only shoot in landscape format unless you get the accessory BH1 ball head. Naturally, with its little legs, you'll be pretty close to the ground if there's nothing available for wrapping around, but you'll be sure to get great camera angles from a worm's eye view.

Cons:

1. Attaching your camera to the tripod is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. A better bet is to get the accessory Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level and attach the quick release clip to your camera beforehand.
2. You need to practice with it a bit to get the stability right, and if you have the legs in an unbalanced position, or on a smooth surface, you can get sagging and camera movement.
3. Trying to get the camera level without the ball head can be quite challenging, and you may well miss the shot. (Of course you can always do the straightening with software, but it's better to get it right the first time.)
4. Can't shoot in portrait format unless you get the ball head.
5. Hard to get the legs back straight with all the segments in line.

Note: It comes with a 1/4-to-3/8-inch adapter attached to the mounting screw, so you have to remove this to attach the camera or accessory ball head.

Recommended (with the [[ASIN:B002CVU4G0 Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level for Joby GP3 SLR-Zoom Gorillapods]]) for photo walks, theme parks or general walk-abouts where that prize-winning shot may be just a Gorillapod away.

I received these as a free review sample eight months ago. Since there are a lot of detailed reviews I will focus on my experience with these and also compare them to other sports phones.

First, these are good quality for twenty buck phones. But do be aware that sports phones are designed for comfort more than sound quality. Not that these are marginal - they have a typical bias towards the mid range, with compressed highs and adequate bass. They are not going to win acclaim from audiophiles, but do reproduce music that is clear and perfect for background listening.

Another thing I like is comfort. I can wear these for a few hours at a time without even noticing them. For sports phones that is a major plus. These allow in a little ambient noise for safety, but it does not appreciably affect the quality of music. Volume is somewhat limited. If you like music super loud these are not going to make you happy. On the other hand, high volume defeats the purpose of sports phones since you need to be aware of ambient noise and your surroundings. I cannot emphasize strongly enough that these are NOT general purpose phones.

Finally, the specs claim about four hours of music play time. That is true with the volume at about a third. If you crank the volume to max you can cut that time in half.

I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. That actually got in the way of using it in a couple of specific places my other projectors can be used at optimal sizes.
That's not to say it gets everything wrong- I DO like that it is small and light and can even be turned on it's back to aim at the ceiling. That's something my big projector can't do, due to the airflow and cable management sticking out the rear. It also has a standard 1/4" 20 threaded tripod mounting point, so you can place this onto a tripod and get maximum mounting freedom. That will come in handy as I've always wanted to watch a movie in bed on the ceiling. But otherwise, don't think this projector will be as good as the other mid-rangers out there. This is still very much a low end projector. You'll have to spend at least 2-3x as much to get a decent home theater style experience, and much more if you want a high end one that will handle FHD/4k to get the real deal. This is more of a specialty use item.

I first bought this GPS several months ago when Costco had it on sale but ended up returning it because I was not pleased with the time it took to recognize my location. More specifically, I would be on the Capital Beltway surrounding DC and the stern female voice would repeatedly tell me to make a U-turn. Impossible. I then used a friend's hand-me-down Magellan which would not hold a charge, not recognize the location and simply needed to be retired. Enter Amazon and their great price for the Navigon 2100 max. Since I'd read that the device was improved with the Fresh Maps update, I purchased Fresh Maps and I highly recommend you do the same if you're contemplating this beautifully sleek GPS.

If you have a PC, you are able to upgrade by connecting the GPS directly to your computer. If you have a Mac, then it's a little more complicated but so worth the effort. You need to remove the SD card from the GPS and transfer the downloaded software to the SD card with a card reader/writer and then reinsert the card into the GPS. I kept a backup of the original software on my hard drive just in case, but have had no need since the upgrade immediately worked. Now on to what I really like about this system.

The 4.3 inch screen is easier to view than the 3.5, particularly if you have many of the POI's selected for display. I first chose them all, then realized they obstructed my map because I'm in the DC metro area. Mine connects with a satellite in only a few seconds each time and reroutes immediately if I change my route. Previously, it would announce that it was rerouting, but it no longer does that, just does the work. Three choices for trip planning are fine enough for me, I tend to choose the Optimal Route. I love being able to select different destinations, too, if I'm going to different places. The address book is easy to access and locations are easier to save. Traffic support is a great asset and now comes free with this device -- I've been saved from many a jam and not have to be tuned into the radio for traffic reports on the 8's. I have the screen set to automatically change from day to night and have had no problem viewing the screen at any time. With the new software, you are able to turn off the GPS from the touchscreen in addition to the usual power button at the upper right hand edge. I love the 2D/3D view, especially when I'm approaching a multi-lane area and I'm unsure as to which lane I need to take. Two voice selections are fine for my needs, Dagmar is more pleasant, but the higher pitched Sarah gives the text to speech option (TTS), so that's the one I've selected. She's not very pushy, either, as some voices I've heard on GPS systems. In the pre-update version, her voice sounded more Germanic, I assume from its origin of Germany, but it's not as odd now. For me, this GPS is intuitive to use and I can make any adjustments from the touchscreen very quickly. I've yet to have a freeze of the system and it has always known where I was with one exception when I was off road on a gravel trail.

Power isn't everything. My intention was for the A90 to replace an old portable DAC/Amp combo that is only rated at 1.6W total at 75Ω. I figured the massive increase in output power paired with a much higher-end DAC would sound heaps better than the little DAC/Amp combo I've been using for the last 7 years. Sadly, the A90 made everything sound a bit thin and lifeless. It's like it has the negative characteristics of an overly clinical sounding amp without any of the positives like extracting detail.

It's not a horrible amp. It's just not a great amp. Maybe the A90 would sound better when paired with muffled/veiled or extremely warm sounding headphones. For Sennheiser HD800's or HD820's though, which are inherently bright, it's a horrible match. The A90 sucked the soul from the music with those particular headphones.

The chain I tested with the A90 was a Naim ND5 XS2 streamer > Nordost Silver Shadow BNC > Schiit Gungnir Multibit DAC > Cardas Clear XLR > Topping A90. There's usually a Schiit Mjolnir 2 at the end of the chain and it sounds amazing. I didn't expect the A90 to outperform the Mjolnir but I did expect it to outperform my little DAC/Amp combo, especially when being fed such a good source

All I can really take away from my experience with the A90 is DO NOT pair this amp with bright headphones. Can't comment on other headphones but avoid this amp if you've got HD800's or 820's.

This case was recommended in several build guides, and seemed to be highly rated on Amazon, but I must say I'm quite disappointed.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. I have some cognitive impairment and mobility challenges from lupus, and I was able to set up Fire TV really easily. The batteries go in the remote; the hdmi cable goes where it goes, and the power plugs in where it plugs in. The screens are responsive with virtually no latency, thanks to the quad core processor and 2 gb ram. And video streaming is also very smooth. I have only been using this a day, but I haven't had it pause to buffer yet. I have a Chromecast in my son's room, a recent model Mac Mini in the living room, an older C2D Mac Mini in my room with Boxee on it, and a Raspberry Pi, and they all buffer at some point during just about every movie. I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. I had come to Amazon to get another Chromecast, but I saw this and thought it would probably be better suited to what I need in my bedroom (I need my husband to be able to watch a tv show without my help - he is completely tech-challenged and cannot work the Dish remote - too many buttons).

The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

Unboxing: Wouldn't usually make a section of this, but every once in a while a product makes it a pleasure. Especially a weird one like this. It's like unboxing a little UFO. It starts out in something like a hat box with a couple sticky tabs of tape to remove. Wish they could have found a better closure method, but the box is nice. Inside that you're immediately presented with the odd looking earbuds and a starter guide (also round) that has you immediately trying them on and fitting the best sleeve size for in your ear. There are no extra sleeves obviously apparent, so time to dig deeper. Next up is the UFO. A large earbud like this needs a large charging case. This one is round and unzips like some of the nicer headphone cases, but it's also a hard case with lights and buttons. Nothing inside but a charging dock. Under it is a secret compartment (made less secret by the thumb holes for easy removal). At the bottom of the hat box we have our missing sleeves and a charging cord.

Even with a diagram, putting these on was confusing and took four tries. Once they're on though, they are quite comfortable, and I think I'll learn to put them on after a few more tries.

Back to the book, and ugh! now they're telling me to put them in the charging case to pair. But I just finally got them on! &*^@#!

Ok, after getting things paired and back on, I'm able to put them through some testing. I'm not really an audiophile, but I've tried a lot of earbuds. Comfort is good. They don't rely on being stuck in your ear to hold themselves up, so there isn't a high stress point that's going to get sore first. They sound good. Better than most, but not the best I've heard. The control button is on the back of your ear, and I find it awkward and unreliable. Noise cancellation is solid, but like every other one I've tried, it is hard to tell sometimes because it scales with volume. Turning them on in a noisy room doesn't result in a quiet room, but turning up what you are listening to will result in noise other than what you are listening to disappearing quite a lot. There is a passthrough mode if you need to hear what's going on around you, but it doesn't sound very nice.

I like that it's USB-C. No more having to turn the cord over three times to figure out which end is up, and much faster charging. The case has three lights to show you charge progress for the case Each one represents enough charge for one full use of the earbuds. Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

This is the second "Creative" brand wireless bluetooth speaker with microphone, and so far, the sound quality has not been very good. The first, "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone" was $127.04 (list price $149.99), and this one currently has a list price of $199.99. I cannot hear any discernable difference in sound quality, though this speaker is larger than the other. They are both OK for being usb powered, but there are better-sounding products out there for the same price if you are willing to sacrifice the speaker option.

I ran the same tests on this speaker as the other and got identical results:

This one gets a mixed review for the overall sound quality, but it does have some features that make it very useful. I will be reviewing its various features individually so you can better assess if this meets your needs or not. I used a decibel measuring app on my phone to determine when the speakers began to distort some of what I played.

Playing audio with Bluetooth or via USB with a computer:
-There is no noticeable difference with playback using Bluetooth versus USB connection to a computer, and it has a Very long range (I walked about 25ft away and it was still doing fine)

AUDIO

75 DECIBELS AND UNDER:
Almost all audio was fine: clear, undistorted, and with pretty good clarity (don't expect GREAT quality or clarity. Just Good.) Some types of music fared poorly even at this relatively soft volume. I used "Fortuna from Carmina Burana" to test the system's limits. (YouTube the piece if you want to know which song I refer to--you'll recognize it immediately) The chorus of singers sounded distorted. At higher volumes, even as lot as 85db, it was awful. Other types of music were fine (orchestra music, pop, hip hop, electronica), but sometimes the treble was a bit fuzzy.

75-85 DECIBELS:
This is the maximum volume the speakers can reach with the USB connection, so it can get loud enough for a small-medium party, but not Very loud.
It's hit and miss here. The treble and bass have some problems, especially treble. The clarity diminishes and any nuances in your music will generally get a bit lost or muffled. Choral music, music with higher pitched percussive elements, and some types of rock and orchestra music don't sound very good.

PHONE CALLS:
The voice of the person you are calling sounds a bit muffled--definitely not as good as headphones or the phone, but about on par with other Bluetooth systems I've tried.

The voice of the speaker (i.e. You) is actually clear! This part gets a solid review. With my built-in car Bluetooth system, as well as detachable ones I've reviewed, usually the person you are calling has trouble hearing you and can experience interference. Maybe that is because it is in the car and there's road noise, but in any case, the fact this one does, actually, sound clear to the recipient of your phone call is a BIG plus.

Overall, this is a good product when you compare it to other desktop laptop speakers. If you are comparing it to products specifically meant for enjoying audio, however, I would recommend the Pioneer Electronics Audition Series for a relatively inexpensive but high quality experience, or Bose if you are looking for something higher-end. The price of the Pioneer product is almost the same, and while it doesn't have Bluetooth unless you buy the attachment separately (about $70) and it only docks with the older iPhone and iPods, the sound quality of that one is stunning. If you want extra features like FREE Bluetooth and speakerphone capability, this one is ok for the price. Not great. Just ok.

Because this is basically the same as the "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone", and the other is about $70 cheaper, I would recommend getting the SBX10 and saving your money. They are basically the same thing, so either pay more and get better sound quality with another product entirely, or pay less for the same thing.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. This GE Universal Remote Control with Roku or Fire TV Streaming Remote Compartment was quite a confusing listing until after I had read it and studied the images a few times. By then, I had already ordered it, thinking it was going to control both my TLC TV and Firestick. Instead, I learned it controls my TV, and just holds my Firestick control on the other side of the remote. But, after thinking about it, I thought, this could actually help keep me from always losing my remotes.
I have to say that setting it up with my TV was a breeze. I don't have cable, only a TLC Roku TV and a Firestick, so no need for all the numbers and other things on the remote. That's a lot of unused buttons...
Well, it would've been ok, if I didn't keep hitting the buttons on the TV side every time I am trying to use my Firestick remote on the other side. It is almost inevitable. Somehow, I always hit a button that takes me to my TLC TV's home screen and exits the Firestick app and, of course, the show I'm watching.
It is also very bulky to just control two devices, or even its purported four. It is actually huge compared to just having both remotes, which I really still have, but in a more complicated form. There are so many more buttons that I'll never use and so much real estate for such a device. Now, if it really did have the ability to control my Firestick built into the other side, that would probably make it more stable, I would think. 
Bottom line, it is just not worth the money, to me, to use it with the "two remotes" feature. Especially, when you're always exiting the show you're watching by hitting a button on the TV side of the remote, when you're only trying to hit pause on the Firestick/Other remote side. I am disappointed in myself, but more so in this device. It could have actually worked out to be a benefit, but it is just a big hassle. It is not my favorite.
